title: Acids, Alkalis and Salts
strapline: The pH scale, neutralisation, and making a salt you can hold in your hand.
bigIdea: Acids and alkalis are opposites that cancel each other out. Neutralisation is one reaction pattern that explains indigestion tablets, soil treatment and salt production alike.
priorKnowledge: Unit 3: metal and non-metal oxides and their acidity.
futureLearning: GCSE: strong and weak acids, titrations, preparing pure dry salt samples, ionic equations for neutralisation.

misconceptions.misconception: All acids are dangerous and all alkalis are safe.
misconceptions.whyItSticks: Film and media portray acid as uniquely corrosive.
misconceptions.addressIt: Compare citric acid (in food) with sodium hydroxide (severely corrosive); establish that concentration, not the label acid or alkali, governs hazard.

misconceptions.misconception: Neutral means nothing is there, or means pure water only.
misconceptions.addressIt: Show that a salt solution made by neutralisation is neutral yet full of dissolved substance.

misconceptions.misconception: A higher pH number always means a stronger, more dangerous chemical.
misconceptions.whyItSticks: Pupils read the scale as a single danger axis.
misconceptions.addressIt: Plot the scale on the board as two directions from 7; ask which is more hazardous, pH 1 or pH 14, to force the two-ended reading.

misconceptions.misconception: The salt produced in neutralisation is table salt.
misconceptions.whyItSticks: Everyday meaning of the word salt.
misconceptions.addressIt: Make copper sulfate crystals and ask whether they would put it on their chips; define salt as a family of compounds.

keyVocabulary.definition: A substance with a pH below 7 that produces hydrogen ions in solution.
A soluble base with a pH above 7.
The reaction between an acid and a base producing a salt and water.
A substance that changes colour depending on the pH.
The compound formed when the hydrogen in an acid is replaced by a metal.
Able to destroy or damage living tissue or materials on contact.

practicals.title: Testing the pH of household substances
apparatus: samples: vinegar, lemon juice, washing soda, soap solution, bicarbonate, water
hazards: Washing soda solution is an irritant
control: Goggles; no tasting of any substance under any circumstances; wash hands afterwards

practicals.title: Following a neutralisation with indicator
hazards: Sodium hydroxide is corrosive even when dilute — eye risk
control: Goggles compulsory and checked before dispensing
Use 0.1 mol/dm3 or weaker; fill burettes below eye level with a funnel

practicals.title: Making copper sulfate crystals
control: Warm the acid gently, never boil
Stop heating while liquid remains; crystallise on a windowsill
practicals.timing: 50 minutes over one or two lessons

practicals.title: Acid plus metal and the hydrogen test
hazards: Hydrogen is flammable — small quantities only
Exothermic reaction with magnesium warms the tube
control: Goggles; use test tube quantities only, never a large flask
Light the splint away from the acid bottles; no naked flames near the hydrogen supply

formative: pH prediction before testing, then compare.
General equation drill: acid + metal -> ? and acid + base -> ?
Salt-naming rapid quiz from acid and metal names.

summative.title: Acids and Alkalis assessment
summative.style: 30 marks, 45 minutes, including a required-practical style method question and a results-interpretation question.
summative.markSchemeNotes: In the method question credit control of variables and a named safety precaution linked to a specific hazard, not generic 'be careful'.

lessons.title: The pH scale and indicators
objectives: Explain why pH 1 and pH 14 are both hazardous
retrieval: Are metal oxides acidic or basic?

sequence.detail: Recall of Unit 3 oxide behaviour.
The pH scale drawn as two directions from neutral; universal indicator colours; distinction between strong and concentrated flagged but not developed.
Test eight household substances; predict first, then measure; record in a results table.
Discuss surprises; address the 'acids are dangerous, alkalis are safe' misconception directly with the oven cleaner example.

keyQuestions: Which is more hazardous, pH 1 or pH 14?
Why is a colour chart needed rather than just 'it went red'?
support: Results table with substances pre-listed and a colour key at the bench.
challenge: Research why red cabbage works as an indicator and make a prediction about its colour at pH 9.
lessons.homework: Annotate a pH scale with five named substances.
lessons.exitTicket: State the pH of a neutral substance and name one.

lessons.title: Neutralisation
objectives: Write the general equation for acid plus base
retrieval: State the pH of an acid, an alkali and a neutral solution

sequence.detail: pH recall, four items.
Acid + base -> salt + water established as a pattern; three worked examples; naming the salt from the acid.
Add alkali to acid drop by drop with universal indicator; record the colour sequence and identify the neutral point.
Apply to indigestion remedies and lime on acidic soil.

keyQuestions: What is present in the flask at exactly pH 7?
Why does adding more alkali past neutral raise the pH?
support: Colour-sequence strip to annotate rather than construct.
challenge: Sketch a pH-against-volume graph and explain the shape of the steep section.
lessons.homework: Explain how indigestion tablets work, using a word equation.

lessons.title: Acids and metals
objectives: Describe the reaction of an acid with a metal
Relate the vigour of the reaction to reactivity
retrieval: Write the general equation for neutralisation
Which is more reactive, magnesium or zinc?

sequence.detail: General equation and reactivity recall.
Acid + metal -> salt + hydrogen; the squeaky pop test modelled.
Three metals with hydrochloric acid; observe rate of fizzing; test the gas; rank the metals.
Link the ranking back to the displacement results from Unit 4 — same order, different evidence.

keyQuestions: How does the fizzing rate give evidence of reactivity?
support: Observation table with a fizzing scale from 0 to 3.
challenge: Predict and justify the reaction of calcium with hydrochloric acid, including a hazard assessment.
lessons.homework: Word equations for four acid-metal reactions.
lessons.exitTicket: Describe the test for hydrogen and its positive result.

lessons.title: Naming and making salts
objectives: Name the salt produced by a given acid and metal
Plan a method to make a named salt
retrieval: Name the salt made from hydrochloric acid and sodium.

sequence.detail: Four salt-naming questions.
Naming rules: hydrochloric gives chlorides, sulfuric gives sulfates, nitric gives nitrates. Twelve examples drilled.
Pupils write a method to make copper sulfate from copper oxide and sulfuric acid, including a hazard column.
Compare plans against a model method; refine before next lesson's practical.

keyQuestions: Why do we add excess copper oxide?
How do we know the reaction has finished?
support: Method steps supplied on cards to sequence rather than write from scratch.
challenge: Suggest how to obtain a pure dry sample and how to check its purity.
lessons.homework: Name the salts from twelve acid and metal combinations.
lessons.exitTicket: Name the salt made from nitric acid and magnesium.

lessons.title: Making copper sulfate crystals
objectives: Carry out a salt preparation safely and accurately
Evaluate the purity of the product
retrieval: State the method steps in order
Name one hazard in this practical and its control.

sequence.detail: Method recalled by pupils; hazards and controls elicited and confirmed before any apparatus is issued.
Warm acid, add excess copper oxide, filter, evaporate partially, leave to crystallise.
Predict what the crystals will look like next lesson and what could reduce the yield.

keyQuestions: Why not evaporate to complete dryness?
support: Step cards at the bench; teacher-prepared warm acid.
challenge: Calculate the theoretical yield from the mass of copper oxide used.
lessons.homework: Write up the method in the passive voice with a labelled diagram.
lessons.exitTicket: Give one reason the yield might be lower than expected.

lessons.title: Applying acids and alkalis
objectives: Evaluate data on soil treatment or acid rain
retrieval: Full recall of the three general equations
State the pH of lemon juice.

sequence.detail: Crystals observed and described; equations recalled.
Soil pH and crop yield dataset: plot, describe the pattern, recommend a treatment with justification.
Acid rain: link back to non-metal oxides from Unit 3; effects on limestone buildings and lakes.
Structured extended answer: 'Explain how a farmer should treat acidic soil and why.'

keyQuestions: Could a farmer add too much? What would happen?
support: Graph axes supplied with the first three points plotted.
challenge: Evaluate the reliability of the dataset and identify a confounding variable.
lessons.homework: Six-mark question on acid rain: causes, effects and one mitigation.
lessons.exitTicket: Name the substance added to acidic soil and say why.

lessons.title: Review and assessment

sequence.detail: General equations, salt naming and pH recall from memory.
30-mark assessment including a method question.
Self-assessment of confidence by topic.

support: Periodic table permitted; reader support as per passports.
challenge: Design a method to make a named salt from an acid and a carbonate.
lessons.exitTicket: Which general equation will you revise first?
